description: We are a multidisciplinary team of 6 passionate students and innovators tackling the "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" challenge. Combining skills in Earth science, data analysis, web development, and UI/UX design, we are building an interactive burning activity calendar to help emergency responders track historical fire patterns and anomalies. Our team roster is currently full and ready to innovate!
summary:
Jamra is a free web app that turns more than 20 years of NASA FIRMS fire data into one fair, consistent record, from 2003 to today.

The challenge: in 2012, the sharper VIIRS sensor (375 m) joined the older MODIS (1 km). It detects about 6 times more hotspots for the same fires. Joining the two records raw creates a fake rise. In Palestine, activity looks 24 times higher after 2012.

We used the overlap years to measure a conversion factor for each country and month, with local factors for small areas. That puts the whole MODIS record on the VIIRS scale. We built the model on 2012–2020 and tested it on hidden years 2022–2025. Typical monthly error fell from 87% to 40%. We found 82 of 121 high-fire months, against 5 with raw data.

Users pick any area in eight Mediterranean countries, or draw one. They get a Burning Activity Calendar comparing each month with its usual level. Every value is marked observed or estimated, with its uncertainty. Data download as CSV or PDF, and early-warning alerts refresh from the NASA FIRMS API every 3 hours.

Jamra helps civil protection, firefighters, land managers and scientists see real fire trends, not sensor artefacts.
details:
What it does

Jamra is a free web app. It turns more than 20 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire data into one fair record, from 2003 to today.

The problem: in 2012 the VIIRS sensor (375 m pixels) joined MODIS (1 km pixels). VIIRS detects about 6 times more hotspots for the same fires. Joining the two records raw creates a fake rise. In Palestine, activity looks 24 times higher after 2012.

How it works

  1. Clean. We remove low-confidence detections. We also remove static heat sources such as gas flares and factories: 215 grid cells.
  2. Calibrate. We compare MODIS Aqua with VIIRS during the overlap years. We use Aqua because it passes at the same afternoon time as VIIRS. This gives a VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio for every country and calendar month. Small areas get their own factor, pulled toward their country’s factor when data are scarce.
  3. Convert and test. Every MODIS month before 2012 becomes “VIIRS-equivalent”, with an error range. We compared six models using 2012–2020 only, then tested the chosen one on 2022–2025, years it never saw. Typical monthly error fell from 87% to 40%. We found 82 of 121 high-fire months, against 5 with raw data.
  4. Stay live. Live data refresh from the NASA FIRMS API every 3 hours. When S-NPP stopped on 2 November 2026, the site switched to NOAA-20, with a measured factor of 0.97.

What users get

  • Choose a fire area or a country, draw a polygon, or type coordinates (eight Mediterranean countries).
  • A yearly chart with a Raw/Harmonized switch, plus a validation line.
  • A Burning Activity Calendar (years × months or weeks), with an “anomaly vs usual” view.
  • Five key indicators and a plain-language story for each month.
  • Early-warning alerts, with open JSON/RSS feeds.
  • A Live Data page, a full Validation page, and CSV, PNG and one-page PDF downloads.

Benefits and intended impact

Civil protection, firefighters, land managers, journalists and scientists can see real fire trends instead of sensor artefacts. They can also tell at a glance whether this month is unusual. The goal is better planning, honest reporting, and a record that stays consistent as VIIRS replaces MODIS.

Creativity

Each calendar cell says whether it was observed by VIIRS or estimated from MODIS, and with what uncertainty. We tested NASA’s suggestion to use Fire Radiative Power (FRP) instead of assuming it worked. In our region, counts were more stable (ratio variability 0.40 vs 0.57), so we kept counts. The archive is precomputed, so a 20-year calendar loads instantly while live data keep flowing.

Tools

  • Data pipeline: Python (standard library, PyYAML, pytest).
  • Website: vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with hand-made SVG charts and no chart library. Maps use MapLibre GL with OpenStreetMap; the 3D globe uses three.js with Natural Earth.
  • Hosting and automation: GitHub Actions (live updates every 3 hours, monthly archive rebuild) and GitHub Pages. An optional Cloudflare Worker keeps the API key secret.
  • Offline use: the site is an installable PWA that works partly offline.
  • No special hardware.
  • AI: we used an AI coding assistant (Claude Code). This is disclosed on the website.

Factors we considered

  • Hotspots are not fires or burned area.
  • Clouds and smoke hide fires, and small areas are noisier.
  • Satellite orbits drift over time.
  • In conflict areas, some hotspots may not be fires.
  • Colour-blind-safe palettes, phone use, and honest uncertainty labels.
  • Jamra is a planning and early-warning tool, not an emergency service.
